claim: MERFISH allows genome-scale imaging of RNAs in individual cells in intact tissues.
source: Multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) allows genome-scale imaging of RNAs in individual cells in intact tissues.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known capability of MERFISH.

claim: MERFISH has been applied to image thin-tissue samples of ~10 µm thickness to date.
source: To date, MERFISH has been applied to image thin-tissue samples of ~10 µm thickness.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a limitation of prior MERFISH applications.

claim: The thick-tissue 3D MERFISH imaging method uses confocal microscopy for optical sectioning.
source: Here, we present a thick-tissue three-dimensional (3D) MERFISH imaging method, which uses confocal microscopy for optical sectioning, deep learning for increasing imaging speed and quality, as well as sample preparation and imaging protocol optimized for thick samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a component of the method.

claim: The thick-tissue 3D MERFISH imaging method uses deep learning for increasing imaging speed and quality.
source: Here, we present a thick-tissue three-dimensional (3D) MERFISH imaging method, which uses confocal microscopy for optical sectioning, deep learning for increasing imaging speed and quality, as well as sample preparation and imaging protocol optimized for thick samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a component of the method.

claim: 3D MERFISH was demonstrated on mouse brain tissue sections of up to 200 µm thickness with high detection efficiency and accuracy.
source: We demonstrated 3D MERFISH on mouse brain tissue sections of up to 200 µm thickness with high detection efficiency and accuracy.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a result of the study.

claim: Spatial genomics enables in situ gene-expression profiling of complex tissues with high spatial resolution.
source: Spatial genomics enables in situ gene-expression profiling of complex tissues with high spatial resolution, allowing for the identification and spatial mapping of molecularly defined cell types in intact tissues (Bressan et al., 2023; Larsson et al., 2021; Zhuang, 2021; Close et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Spatial genomics allows for the identification and spatial mapping of molecularly defined cell types in intact tissues.
source: Spatial genomics enables in situ gene-expression profiling of complex tissues with high spatial resolution, allowing for the identification and spatial mapping of molecularly defined cell types in intact tissues (Bressan et al., 2023; Larsson et al., 2021; Zhuang, 2021; Close et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Imaging-based approaches allow simultaneous visualization and quantification of hundreds to thousands of genes in individual cells.
source: (1) imaging-based approaches that allow simultaneous visualization and quantification of hundreds to thousands of genes in individual cells
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a characteristic of imaging-based spatial genomics approaches.

claim: Next-generation sequencing-based methods use nucleic acid barcodes to encode positional information onto transcripts, followed by sequencing to determine both the genetic identity and spatial location of the transcripts.
source: (2) next-generation sequencing-based methods, which use nucleic acid barcodes to encode positional information onto transcripts, followed by sequencing to determine both the genetic identity and spatial location of the transcripts (Bressan et al., 2023; Larsson et al., 2021; Zhuang, 2021).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Spatial genomics approaches have been mainly applied to thin-tissue sections of 10–20 µm thickness.
source: These approaches have been mainly applied to thin-tissue sections of 10–20 µm thickness.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a limitation of current approaches.

claim: Many functional and anatomical studies of biological systems require volumetric measurement of thick-tissue blocks.
source: However, many functional and anatomical studies of biological systems require volumetric measurement of thick-tissue blocks.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a motivation for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: It is challenging to align serial thin-section images due to tissue deformation that occurs during sectioning.
source: In practice, it is challenging to align these serial-section images due to the tissue deformation that occurs during sectioning, which in turn makes it more challenging to accurately determine the 3D morphology and organization of cells within tissues.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a challenge with serial sectioning.

claim: Tissue deformation during sectioning makes it challenging to accurately determine the 3D morphology and organization of cells within tissues.
source: In practice, it is challenging to align these serial-section images due to the tissue deformation that occurs during sectioning, which in turn makes it more challenging to accurately determine the 3D morphology and organization of cells within tissues.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a consequence of tissue deformation.

claim: Multimodal characterizations of cells in tissues often require registration of transcriptomic images with images that capture other cellular properties through thick-tissue or live-animal imaging.
source: Additionally, multimodal characterizations of the molecular, morphological, and functional properties of cells in tissues often require registration of transcriptomic images with images that capture other cellular properties through thick-tissue or live-animal imaging, such as neuronal activity imaging.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a motivation for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: Alignment of multiple thin-section transcriptomic images with thick-tissue or live-animal volumetric images poses significant challenges.
source: Alignment of multiple thin-section transcriptomic images with such thick-tissue or live-animal volumetric images also poses significant challenges.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a challenge with thin-section imaging.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated 3D gene-expression profiling of dozens of genes in intact tissues with thicknesses ranging from 100 to 300 µm.
source: Recent studies (Nobori et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021) have demonstrated the 3D gene-expression profiling of dozens of genes in intact tissues with thicknesses ranging from 100 to 300 µm.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The vast majority of today's spatial transcriptomic measurements are derived from tissues with thicknesses of only 10–20 µm.
source: Despite these advancements, the vast majority of today's spatial transcriptomic measurements are still derived from tissues with thicknesses of only 10–20 µm, largely due to the scarcity of methods capable of thick-tissue 3D transcriptomic measurements.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a current limitation.

claim: The scarcity of methods capable of thick-tissue 3D transcriptomic measurements is the reason most spatial transcriptomic measurements are derived from thin tissues.
source: Despite these advancements, the vast majority of today's spatial transcriptomic measurements are still derived from tissues with thicknesses of only 10–20 µm, largely due to the scarcity of methods capable of thick-tissue 3D transcriptomic measurements.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a causal relationship.

claim: MERFISH is a single-cell genome-scale imaging method that allows simultaneously imaging and qualification of RNAs from thousands of genes.
source: MERFISH is a single-cell genome-scale imaging method that allows simultaneously imaging and qualification of RNAs from thousands of genes (Chen et al., 2015; Xia et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MERFISH has been extended to allow spatially resolved 3D-genome imaging and epigenomic profiling of individual cells.
source: MERFISH has also been extended to allow spatially resolved 3D-genome imaging and epigenomic profiling of individual cells (Lu et al., 2022; Su et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MERFISH measurements have only been conducted on thin-tissue sections of ~10 µm in thickness so far.
source: So far, MERFISH measurements have only been conducted on thin-tissue sections of ~10 µm in thickness.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a limitation of prior MERFISH work.

claim: Fluorescence background caused by out-of-focus signals reduces image quality in thick-tissue imaging.
source: First, the fluorescence background caused by out-of-focus signals reduces image quality.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a challenge for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: Spherical aberration introduced by refractive-index mismatches leads to degradation in image resolution and quality, particularly in the deeper regions of thick-tissue samples.
source: Second, spherical aberration introduced by refractive-index mismatches leads to degradation in image resolution and quality, particularly in the deeper regions of thick-tissue samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a challenge for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: The gel-based tissue clearing protocol used in tissue MERFISH imaging was originally optimized for thin-tissue imaging and may not be adequate for imaging thick samples.
source: Third, the gel-based tissue clearing protocol, often used in tissue MERFISH imaging, was originally optimized for thin-tissue imaging and may not be adequate for imaging thick samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a challenge for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: Spinning disk confocal microscopy was used to achieve optical sectioning and eliminate out-of-focus fluorescence signals.
source: First, we used spinning disk confocal microscopy to achieve optical sectioning and eliminate the out-of-focus fluorescence signals, which significantly improved the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the MERFISH images of thick-tissue sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by a figure reference.

claim: Spinning disk confocal microscopy significantly improved the signal-to-noise ratio in MERFISH images of thick-tissue sections.
source: First, we used spinning disk confocal microscopy to achieve optical sectioning and eliminate the out-of-focus fluorescence signals, which significantly improved the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the MERFISH images of thick-tissue sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spinning-disk confocal detection geometry cuts a large amount of in-focus fluorescence signals.
source: However, the spinning-disk confocal detection geometry also cuts a large amount of in-focus fluorescence signals, and hence a substantially longer exposure time or higher illumination light intensity is required to achieve a high SNR for imaging individual RNA molecules in the sample.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a limitation of confocal microscopy.

claim: A substantially longer exposure time or higher illumination light intensity is required to achieve a high SNR for imaging individual RNA molecules in confocal microscopy.
source: However, the spinning-disk confocal detection geometry also cuts a large amount of in-focus fluorescence signals, and hence a substantially longer exposure time or higher illumination light intensity is required to achieve a high SNR for imaging individual RNA molecules in the sample.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a consequence of confocal detection geometry.

claim: Longer exposure time or higher illumination intensity leads to a drastic reduction in imaging speed and/or substantial photobleaching of out-of-focus fluorophores.
source: This leads to a drastic reduction in imaging speed and/or a substantial photobleaching of out-of-focus fluorophores before they are imaged.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a consequence of the confocal approach.

claim: Deep learning has been used to improve the quality of fluorescence microscopy images in various applications.
source: We reasoned that deep learning, which has been used to improve the quality of fluorescence microscopy images in various applications (Laine et al., 2021; Ouyang et al., 2018; Weigert et al., 2018), could potentially improve the SNR of confocal MERFISH images acquired at high speed or with low illumination intensity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: 242 genes were measured in tissue sections of the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: To test this approach, we performed MERFISH imaging to measure 242 genes (Supplementary file 1–3) in tissue sections of the mouse cerebral cortex, imaging the same fields of view (FOVs) with both a long (1 s) and a short (0.1 s) exposure time per frame to obtain high and low SNR image pairs, respectively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as part of the experimental design.

claim: The same fields of view were imaged with both a long (1 s) and a short (0.1 s) exposure time per frame to obtain high and low SNR image pairs.
source: To test this approach, we performed MERFISH imaging to measure 242 genes (Supplementary file 1–3) in tissue sections of the mouse cerebral cortex, imaging the same fields of view (FOVs) with both a long (1 s) and a short (0.1 s) exposure time per frame to obtain high and low SNR image pairs, respectively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as part of the experimental design.

claim: Low-SNR MERFISH images acquired with 0.1 s exposure time led to a substantially lower (4× lower) detection efficiency compared to high-SNR measurement acquired at 1 s exposure time.
source: As expected, the low-SNR MERFISH images acquired with 0.1 s exposure time led to a substantially lower (4× lower) detection efficiency compared to the high-SNR measurement acquired at the 1 s exposure time (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1a and b.

claim: A neural network was trained based on a subset of short- and long-exposure-time image pairs to improve the quality of images taken with short exposure time.
source: To test whether deep learning can enhance the quality of the 0.1 s images, we trained a neural network based on a subset of the short- and long-exposure-time image pairs and subsequently used this model to improve the quality of the remaining images taken with the short-exposure time (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as part of the experimental approach.

claim: Deep learning improved the SNR of the 0.1 s images substantially.
source: This approach indeed improved the SNR of the 0.1 s images substantially (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1c.

claim: The detection accuracy and efficiency of MERFISH images acquired with 0.1 s exposure time became nearly identical to that measured with 1 s exposure time after deep learning enhancement.
source: As a result, the detection accuracy and efficiency of MERFISH images acquired with 0.1 s exposure time were increased and became nearly identical to that measured with 1 s exposure time (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1d.

claim: Deep learning allowed acquisition of high-quality confocal MERFISH images at high speed under low illumination intensity.
source: This allowed us to acquire high-quality confocal MERFISH images at high speed under low illumination intensity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion from the deep learning results.

claim: It is important to avoid aberration caused by refractive-index mismatch in thick-tissue imaging.
source: In thick-tissue imaging, it is important to avoid aberration caused by refractive-index mismatch.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a consideration for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: High numerical-aperture (NA = 1.4) oil-immersion objectives were previously used for thin-tissue MERFISH imaging.
source: We have previously used high numerical-aperture (NA = 1.4) oil-immersion objectives for thin-tissue MERFISH imaging.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as prior practice.

claim: High NA oil-immersion objectives have high detection efficiency of fluorescence signals from thin samples close to the glass substrate.
source: While these objectives have a high detection efficiency of fluorescence signals from thin samples close to the glass substrate, they present significant challenges when imaging thick samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a characteristic of oil-immersion objectives.

claim: High NA oil-immersion objectives present significant challenges when imaging thick samples.
source: While these objectives have a high detection efficiency of fluorescence signals from thin samples close to the glass substrate, they present significant challenges when imaging thick samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a limitation for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: Refractive-index mismatch between immersion oil and tissue samples leads to substantial aberration, which reduces the sensitivity and accuracy of RNA detection in deeper regions of thick samples.
source: The refractive-index mismatch between the immersion oil and tissue samples leads to substantial aberration, which reduces the sensitivity and accuracy of RNA detection in the deeper regions of thick samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a problem with oil-immersion objectives.

claim: Water-immersion objectives were used to overcome the refractive-index mismatch problem.
source: To overcome this problem, we switched to water-immersion objectives, which have a better refractive-index match with the samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a solution to the aberration problem.

claim: Water-immersion objectives have a better refractive-index match with tissue samples than oil-immersion objectives.
source: To overcome this problem, we switched to water-immersion objectives, which have a better refractive-index match with the samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a rationale for using water objectives.

claim: Water-immersion objectives have a lower NA (NA = 1.15 or 1.2) than oil-immersion objectives.
source: Despite having a lower NA (NA = 1.15 or 1.2), these water objectives allowed for the detection of individual RNA molecules without substantial decay of detection sensitivity and efficiency across the entire depth of 100-µm- and 200-µm-thick-tissue sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a characteristic of water objectives.

claim: Water objectives allowed for the detection of individual RNA molecules without substantial decay of detection sensitivity and efficiency across the entire depth of 100-µm- and 200-µm-thick-tissue sections.
source: Despite having a lower NA (NA = 1.15 or 1.2), these water objectives allowed for the detection of individual RNA molecules without substantial decay of detection sensitivity and efficiency across the entire depth of 100-µm- and 200-µm-thick-tissue sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gel-based tissue clearing is often used for MERFISH imaging of tissue samples.
source: Finally, we often use gel-based tissue clearing for MERFISH imaging of tissue samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a common practice.

claim: The gel-based MERFISH protocol developed using thin-tissue samples needed to be optimized for imaging thick-tissue samples.
source: Our gel-based MERFISH protocol developed using thin-tissue samples also need to be optimized for imaging thick-tissue samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a requirement for thick-tissue imaging.

claim: In MERFISH, cellular RNAs are labeled with a library of encoding oligonucleotide probes that contains barcode-determining readout sequences.
source: In MERFISH, we label cellular RNAs with a library of encoding oligonucleotide probes that contains barcode-determining readout sequences and then detect the barcodes bit-by-bit with dye-labeled readout probes complementary to the readout sequences (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Barcodes are detected bit-by-bit with dye-labeled readout probes complementary to the readout sequences in MERFISH.
source: In MERFISH, we label cellular RNAs with a library of encoding oligonucleotide probes that contains barcode-determining readout sequences and then detect the barcodes bit-by-bit with dye-labeled readout probes complementary to the readout sequences (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The encoding and readout probe labeling conditions previously developed for thin-tissue imaging may not be optimal for thick-tissue imaging.
source: The encoding and readout probe labeling conditions previously developed for thin-tissue imaging may not be optimal for thick-tissue imaging.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a consideration for protocol optimization.

claim: 242 genes were imaged in 100-µm-thick mouse brain sections with 1 µm step size for each z-plane.
source: To optimize the MERFISH protocol for thick-tissue imaging, we imaged the 242 genes in 100-µm-thick mouse brain sections with 1 µm step size for each z-plane.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as part of the optimization process.

claim: Bright and consistent signals from individual RNA molecules were observed across the entire depth of 100-µm-thick-tissue samples in each bit upon optimization of probe labeling conditions.
source: Upon optimization of probe labeling conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d), we observed bright and consistent signals from individual RNA molecules across the entire depth of 100-µm-thick-tissue samples in each bit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The copy number of RNA molecules identified for individual genes decreased substantially with tissue depth despite consistent detection of RNA molecules in individual bits.
source: However, unexpectedly, despite consistent detection of RNA molecules in individual bits, the copy number of RNA molecules identified for individual genes decreased substantially with the tissue depth and exhibited a poor correlation with bulk RNA-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–c.

claim: The decrease in RNA copy number with tissue depth may be due to displacement of RNA molecules between imaging rounds in thick-tissue samples.
source: We reasoned that this may be due to the displacement of RNA molecules between imaging rounds in the thick-tissue sample that made these molecules difficult to decode and identify from their multibit images.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a hypothesis to explain the observation.

claim: Significant displacement in the positions of fiducial beads was observed in all three dimensions (x, y, and z) between imaging rounds, especially in the deeper part of thick-tissue samples.
source: To test this, we imaged fiducial beads embedded in the polyacrylamide gel, which is often used for sample clearing in MERFISH imaging of tissue samples (Moffitt et al., 2016a). Indeed, we observed a significant displacement in the positions of beads in all three dimensions (x, y, and z) between imaging rounds, especially in the deeper part of the thick-tissue samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claim: Three factors contribute to the displacement of RNA molecule positions between imaging rounds: piezo-actuator inconsistency, gel expansion/shrinkage upon buffer changes, and axial chromatic aberration.
source: We identified three factors contributing to the displacement of RNA molecule positions between imaging rounds: (1) the piezo-actuator used for z-scanning of the objective did not consistently place the focal plane at defined z-positions of the sample during each imaging round; (2) the MERFISH protocol includes multiple buffer-exchange steps, and the expansion or shrinkage of the polyacrylamide gel upon buffer changes contributed to the displacement of RNA molecules across imaging rounds; and (3) two-color imaging was used to measure two bits in each hybridization round, and the axial chromatic aberration between the two colors resulted in misalignment of RNA molecules between bits measured in different color channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as identified factors.

claim: The Queensgate OP400 piezo demonstrated the highest precision and reproducibility among various piezo actuators tested.
source: To solve the first problem, we conducted tests using various piezo actuators and chose the Queensgate OP400 piezo, which demonstrated the highest precision and reproducibility.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a solution to the piezo problem.

claim: The Queensgate OP400 piezo provided negligible z-position error for sample thicknesses under 200 µm.
source: This specific piezo provided negligible z-position error for sample thicknesses under 200 µm.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a characteristic of the chosen piezo.

claim: A low concentration of gel initiator and low polymerization temperature (4°C) were used to generate polyacrylamide gel with a lower degree of buffer-dependent expansion.
source: To minimize the gel expansion effect, we used a low concentration of gel initiator and low polymerization temperature (4°C) to generate polyacrylamide gel with a lower degree of buffer-dependent expansion (Boyde, 1976) and chose MERFISH buffers that further minimize the gel-expansion effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a and b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a supporting citation and figure reference.

claim: MERFISH buffers were chosen to further minimize the gel-expansion effect.
source: To minimize the gel expansion effect, we used a low concentration of gel initiator and low polymerization temperature (4°C) to generate polyacrylamide gel with a lower degree of buffer-dependent expansion (Boyde, 1976) and chose MERFISH buffers that further minimize the gel-expansion effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a and b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3a and b.

claim: The gel was allowed to relax for an extra 10 min following buffer exchange to the imaging buffer to ensure it recovered to the same size before imaging.
source: In addition, to ensure that the gel recovered to the same size before imaging, the gel was allowed to relax for an extra 10 min following buffer exchange to the imaging buffer in order to completely remove any residual gel expansion induced by other buffers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Axial chromatic aberration was calibrated by imaging fiducial beads in the two-color channels to allow precise alignment of images between these channels.
source: To eliminate the effect of chromatic aberration, we calibrated the axial chromatic aberration by imaging fiducial beads in the two-color channels, which allowed precise alignment of images between these channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a solution to the chromatic aberration problem.

claim: The expression of 242 genes was imaged in 100-µm-thick sections of the mouse cortex to validate the optimized thick-tissue MERFISH protocol.
source: To validate our optimized thick-tissue MERFISH protocol, we first imaged the expression of the 242 genes in 100-µm-thick sections of the mouse cortex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a validation experiment.

claim: Nuclear DAPI stain and total polyadenylated mRNA signals were imaged for 3D cell segmentation in addition to MERFISH imaging of RNAs.
source: In addition to MERFISH imaging of RNAs, we also imaged the nuclear DAPI stain and total polyadenylated mRNA signals for 3D cell segmentation (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2a.

claim: Individual RNA molecules were clearly identified in the thick-tissue MERFISH images.
source: Individual RNA molecules were clearly identified in the thick-tissue MERFISH images (Figure 2b and c, Figure 2—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: The average RNA copy numbers for individual genes were highly correlated with the RNA abundance measured by bulk RNA sequencing.
source: The average RNA copy numbers for individual genes were highly correlated with the RNA abundance measured by bulk RNA sequencing (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2d.

claim: The detected RNA number and the correlation with bulk RNA-seq did not show any decay across the entire tissue depth.
source: The detected RNA number and the correlation with bulk RNA-seq did not show any decay across the entire tissue depth (Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2e and f.

claim: The detection efficiency of confocal thick-tissue measurements per z-plane was ~20% higher than the epi thin-tissue measurements.
source: We then compared the RNA copy number of individual genes detected per unit area per z-plane with the results from 10-µm-thin-tissue MERFISH measurements performed previously using an epifluorescence setup (Zhang et al., 2021). The detection efficiency of confocal thick-tissue measurements per z-plane was ~20% higher than the epi thin-tissue measurements (Figure 2g), which may be due to the background reduction by confocal optical sectioning.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2g.

claim: The higher detection efficiency of confocal thick-tissue measurements may be due to background reduction by confocal optical sectioning.
source: The detection efficiency of confocal thick-tissue measurements per z-plane was ~20% higher than the epi thin-tissue measurements (Figure 2g), which may be due to the background reduction by confocal optical sectioning.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a possible explanation.

claim: The RNA copy number per cell detected in 100-µm-thick samples was twofold higher than that obtained from individual 10-µm-thick sections of the same sample.
source: When we compared the RNA copy number per cell detected in the 100-µm-thick samples with the results obtained from individual 10-µm-thick sections of the same sample (obtained by dividing the 100 µm z-range into 10 equal-thickness sections), we found that the former was twofold higher than the latter (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 2h.

claim: Most cell bodies were completely captured within 100-µm-thick tissues, whereas many cells were only partially captured in 10-µm-thick-tissue sections.
source: This is presumably because most of the cell bodies were completely captured within the 100-µm-thick tissues, whereas many cells were only partially captured in the 10-µm-thick-tissue sections.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an explanation for the twofold difference.

claim: Normalization of RNA copy number by cell volume could partially mitigate the problem of partial cell capture in thin-tissue imaging.
source: Although normalization of the RNA copy number by cell volume could partially mitigate this problem in thin-tissue imaging, detecting too few RNA molecules per cell could nonetheless introduce significant noise and imposing a cell volume threshold to reduce noise would in turn reduce the number of cells measured.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a limitation of normalization approaches.

claim: Detecting too few RNA molecules per cell could introduce significant noise.
source: Although normalization of the RNA copy number by cell volume could partially mitigate this problem in thin-tissue imaging, detecting too few RNA molecules per cell could nonetheless introduce significant noise and imposing a cell volume threshold to reduce noise would in turn reduce the number of cells measured.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a problem with thin-tissue imaging.

claim: Imposing a cell volume threshold to reduce noise would reduce the number of cells measured.
source: Although normalization of the RNA copy number by cell volume could partially mitigate this problem in thin-tissue imaging, detecting too few RNA molecules per cell could nonetheless introduce significant noise and imposing a cell volume threshold to reduce noise would in turn reduce the number of cells measured.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a trade-off in thin-tissue imaging.

claim: Nonuniform intracellular distribution of RNAs could reduce transcriptome profiling accuracy when only part of a cell is imaged.
source: Moreover, nonuniform intracellular distribution of RNAs could further reduce transcriptome profiling accuracy when only part of a cell is imaged.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an additional problem with partial cell capture.

claim: Thick-tissue MERFISH imaging should allow more accurate gene-expression profiling of individual cells.
source: Thus, thick-tissue MERFISH imaging should allow more accurate gene-expression profiling of individual cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion from the comparison.

claim: Single-cell expression profiles derived from 3D thick-tissue MERFISH measurement were used to identify transcriptionally distinct cell populations in the mouse cortex.
source: Next, we used single-cell expression profiles derived from our 3D thick-tissue MERFISH measurement to identify transcriptionally distinct cell populations in the mouse cortex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an analysis performed.

claim: All previously known subclasses of excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, and non-neuronal cells were observed in the mouse cortex.
source: We observed all previously known subclasses of excitatory neurons (layer 2/3 [L2/3] intratelencephalic-projection neurons [L2/3 IT], L4/5 IT, L5 IT, L6 IT, L6 Car3 neurons, L5 extratelencephalic projection neurons [L5 ET], L5/6 near projection neurons [L5/6 NP], L6 cortical-thalamic projection neurons [L6 CT], and L6b neurons), inhibitory neurons (marked by Lamp5, Sst, Vip, Pvalb, and Sncg, respectively), and non-neuronal cells (oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, astrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, pericytes, vascular leptomeningeal cells, smooth muscle cells) (Figure 3a), as well as transcriptionally distinct cell clusters within these subclasses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 3D MERFISH images showed the expected layered organization of transcriptionally distinct neuronal cell populations in the cortex.
source: The 3D MERFISH images further showed the expected layered organization of transcriptionally distinct neuronal cell populations in the cortex (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3b.

claim: 156 genes were measured in a 200-µm-thick section of the mouse anterior hypothalamus.
source: To test if our thick-tissue 3D MERFISH approach can image beyond 100 µm thickness, we next measured 156 genes (Supplementary files 4 and 5) in a 200-µm-thick section of the mouse anterior hypothalamus.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an experiment to test thicker samples.

claim: The RNA copy numbers of individual genes measured per cell per z-plane at different tissue depths showed excellent correlation with each other with only a slight reduction across the entire tissue depth in the 200-µm-thick section.
source: The RNA copy numbers of individual genes measured per cell per z-plane at different tissue depths showed excellent correlation with each other with only a slight reduction of the RNA copy number across the entire tissue depth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 21 excitatory neuronal clusters, 26 inhibitory neuronal clusters, and 7 non-neuronal cell subclasses were identified in the mouse anterior hypothalamus.
source: From the MERFISH-derived single-cell expression profiles, we identified 21 excitatory neuronal clusters, 26 inhibitory neuronal clusters, and 7 non-neuronal cell subclasses in this region (Figure 3c and d, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: Most transcriptionally distinct neuronal clusters showed distinct and localized spatial distributions in the hypothalamus.
source: Most of the transcriptionally distinct neuronal clusters showed distinct and localized spatial distributions, some of which were predominantly located in a single hypothalamic nucleus such as inhibitory cluster I1 in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, inhibitory cluster I5 in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, and excitatory cluster E20 in the nucleus of reuniens thalamic (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: The same type of interneurons tend to form juxtaposed pairs in the mouse visual cortex.
source: It has been shown previously that the same type of interneurons (Lamp5, Vip, Sst, or Pvalb-positive inhibitory neurons) tend to form juxtaposed pairs in the mouse visual cortex (Wang et al., 2018) and human middle and superior temporal gyrus (Fang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Tightly juxtaposed interneuron structures might be mediated by electric gap junctions, which is important for synchronized firing patterns.
source: It has been hypothesized that such tightly juxtaposed structures might be mediated by electric gap junctions, which is important for synchronized firing patterns (Amitai et al., 2002; Gibson et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The distances between nearest-neighbor pairs of interneurons of the same type were significantly smaller than the distances between nearest-neighbor pairs of an interneuron and a different type of neuron in the mouse cortex.
source: We found that the distances between the former category of nearest-neighbor pairs were significantly smaller than the distances between the latter category of nearest-neighbor pairs, even though the density of interneurons in the cortex is substantially lower than that of the excitatory neurons (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3e.

claim: A bimodal distribution of nearest-neighbor distances among all inhibitory neurons was observed in the mouse cortex, with a significant fraction of distances falling in a peak less than 10 μm.
source: We observed a bimodal distribution: while the major peak was centered at about 30 μm, a significant fraction of nearest-neighbor distances fell in a peak that was <10 μm (marked by arrow in Figure 3f).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3f.

claim: Interneurons with nearest-neighbor distances less than 10 μm were not only juxtaposed but also formed junctions so tight that led to morphological deformations of the cell bodies.
source: Visualization of these latter interneurons in the MERFISH images suggests that they were not only juxtaposed but also formed junctions so tight that led to morphological deformations of the cell bodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The median distance between tightly juxtaposed interneurons was less than 10 µm even though the average diameter of a single interneuron was approximately 15 µm.
source: As a result, the median distance between those interneurons was less than 10 µm even though the average diameter of a single interneuron was approximately 15 µm (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 4b.

claim: The results are consistent with previous observations that interneurons tend to form tightly juxtaposed pairs in the mouse and human cortex.
source: These results are consistent with previous observation that interneurons tend to form tightly juxtaposed pairs in the mouse and human cortex (Fang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: In the hypothalamus, the distances between nearest-neighboring pairs formed by the same type of interneurons were not significantly smaller than those between nearest-neighboring pairs formed by an interneuron and a neuron of a different type.
source: In the first analysis, we found that the distances between the nearest-neighboring pairs formed by the same type of interneurons were not significantly smaller than those between the nearest-neighboring pairs formed by an interneuron and a neuron of a different type (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3g.

claim: Interneuron subtypes formed tight spatial clusters in the hypothalamus, unlike in the cortex where interneurons formed a scattered distribution.
source: Unlike in the cortex, where the interneurons formed a scattered distribution, the interneuron subtypes formed tight spatial clusters in the hypothalamus (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: The distribution of nearest-neighbor distances among all interneurons in the hypothalamus formed a single-modal distribution centered at a small distance.
source: In the second analysis, we found that the distribution of the nearest-neighbor distances among all interneurons formed a single-modal distribution centered at a small distance (Figure 3h), consistent with the observation of tight spatial clusters of interneuron subtypes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3h.

claim: Tightly juxtaposed interneuron pairs with deformed cell bodies were much rarer in the hypothalamus than in the cortex.
source: While we were also able to find tightly juxtaposed interneuron pairs with deformed cell bodies in the hypothalamus (Figure 3—figure supplement 4c), such examples were much rarer than those in the cortex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 4c.

claim: Interneurons potentially have a lower tendency to form juxtaposed pairs with tight junctions in the hypothalamus than in the cortex.
source: Hence, it appears that interneurons potentially have a lower tendency to form such juxtaposed interneuron pairs with tight junctions in the hypothalamus than in the cortex, but it is also worth noting that the spatially clustered distributions of interneuron subtypes could make it more difficult to detect such tightly juxtaposed interneuron pairs in the mouse hypothalamus quantitatively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a conclusion with a caveat.

claim: The spatially clustered distributions of interneuron subtypes could make it more difficult to detect tightly juxtaposed interneuron pairs in the mouse hypothalamus quantitatively.
source: Hence, it appears that interneurons potentially have a lower tendency to form such juxtaposed interneuron pairs with tight junctions in the hypothalamus than in the cortex, but it is also worth noting that the spatially clustered distributions of interneuron subtypes could make it more difficult to detect such tightly juxtaposed interneuron pairs in the mouse hypothalamus quantitatively.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a caveat to the conclusion.

claim: A method was developed that allowed high-quality 3D MERFISH imaging in thick-tissue samples.
source: In summary, we developed a method that allowed high-quality 3D MERFISH imaging in thick-tissue samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a summary of the work.

claim: One of the major challenges of thick-tissue RNA imaging is the low signal-to-background ratio of individual RNA molecules.
source: One of the major challenges of thick-tissue RNA imaging is the low signal-to-background ratio of individual RNA molecules.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a challenge addressed by the work.

claim: Signal amplification has been previously used for thick-tissue imaging to address the low signal-to-background ratio challenge.
source: To address this challenge, signal amplification has been previously used for thick-tissue imaging.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a prior approach.

claim: In STARmap and PHYTOMap, enzymatic process of rolling circle amplification is used to generate DNA amplicons, thereby enhancing the signals.
source: For example, in STARmap (Wang et al., 2018) and PHYTOMap (Nobori et al., 2023), enzymatic process of rolling circle amplification (Krzywkowski and Nilsson, 2017; Banér et al., 1998) is used to generate DNA amplicons, thereby enhancing the signals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The requirement of enzymes in rolling circle amplification may potentially restrict or slow reagent penetration in thick tissues.
source: However, the requirement of enzymes in this process may potentially restrict or slow reagent penetration in thick tissues.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a limitation of enzymatic amplification.

claim: EASI-FISH employs hybridization chain reaction (HCR) for signal amplification.
source: Alternatively, EASI-FISH (Wang et al., 2021) employs hybridization chain reaction (HCR) (Dirks and Pierce, 2004) for signal amplification.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: HCR oligos are short (50–100 nt) and can potentially penetrate thick tissue more rapidly.
source: Since HCR oligos are short (50–100 nt), they can potentially penetrate thick tissue more rapidly.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an advantage of HCR.

claim: EASI-FISH was originally used to measure the expression of dozens of genes sequentially and the number of genes that can be measured is limited by the number of available HCR amplifiers.
source: This latter approach was originally used to measure the expression of dozens of genes sequentially and the number of genes that can be measured is limited by the number of available HCR amplifiers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a limitation of EASI-FISH.

claim: A bioRxiv preprint reported cycleHCR, a technology that leverages multiplexed barcoding and split HCR, which has enabled the measurement of hundreds of genes within a 300-μm-thick mouse embryo.
source: During the revision of our manuscript, a bioRxiv preprint (Gandin et al., 2024) reported cycleHCR – a technology that leverages multiplexed barcoding and split HCR, which has enabled the measurement of hundreds of genes within a 300-μm-thick mouse embryo.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Another bioRxiv preprint reported approaches that enable 3D in situ quantification of thousands of genes and their corresponding translation activities in 200-μm-thick-tissue blocks using STARmap and RiboMap.
source: Additionally, another bioRxiv preprint (Sui et al., 2024) reported approaches that enable 3D in situ quantification of thousands of genes and their corresponding translation activities in 200-μm-thick-tissue blocks using STARmap and RiboMap.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The challenge of low signal-to-background ratio in thick-tissue imaging was overcome by combining optical sectioning with deep learning, without involving signal amplification.
source: In this work, we overcome the challenge of low signal-to-background ratio in thick-tissue imaging by combining optical sectioning with deep learning, without involving signal amplification.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as the approach taken in this work.

claim: The oligonucleotide probes used in thick-tissue 3D MERFISH approach are only 20-base long, which allows for efficient penetration into thick tissues.
source: The oligonucleotide probes used in our thick-tissue 3D MERFISH approach are only 20-base long, which allows for efficient penetration into thick tissues.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an advantage of the approach.

claim: 3D MERFISH of tissue blocks up to 200 µm was demonstrated in this work.
source: We demonstrated 3D MERFISH of tissue blocks up to 200 µm in this work, and the consistently high performance along the entire tissue depth suggests that our approach can be applied to image thicker tissue samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a result of the work.

claim: The consistently high performance along the entire tissue depth suggests that the approach can be applied to image thicker tissue samples.
source: We demonstrated 3D MERFISH of tissue blocks up to 200 µm in this work, and the consistently high performance along the entire tissue depth suggests that our approach can be applied to image thicker tissue samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an inference from the results.

claim: Imaging thick tissues allows capturing the full cell-body volume of nearly all imaged cells, which increases gene-expression profiling accuracy.
source: For instance, as we have shown here, imaging thick tissues allows us to capture the full cell-body volume of nearly all imaged cells, and hence increases the gene-expression profiling accuracy.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an advantage of thick-tissue imaging.

claim: Confocal imaging removes out-of-focus fluorescence background, which can potentially allow imaging more genes or the same number of genes with fewer imaging rounds.
source: Second, confocal imaging removes out-of-focus fluorescence background, which can potentially allow us to image more genes or the same number of genes with fewer imaging rounds.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as a potential advantage of confocal imaging.

claim: Confocal imaging should facilitate cell segmentation, especially in regions with high cell density.
source: Third, we also anticipate confocal imaging to facilitate cell segmentation, especially in regions with high cell density.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an anticipated advantage.

claim: Thick-tissue imaging should facilitate integrated measurements of gene-expression profiles and morphology of individual cells because the shape of cells can be better determined by volumetric imaging.
source: Fourth, because the shape of cells can be better determined by volumetric imaging, thick-tissue imaging should facilitate integrated measurements of gene-expression profiles and morphology of individual cells to investigate the relationship between these two properties.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an anticipated advantage.

claim: Thick-tissue single-cell transcriptome imaging will facilitate more efficient detection of interactions between molecularly defined cell types.
source: Fifth, thick-tissue single-cell transcriptome imaging will also facilitate more efficient detection of interactions between molecularly defined cell types.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an anticipated advantage.

claim: The approach is envisioned to facilitate combined measurements of neuronal activity with transcriptomic profiling of individual cells to reveal the functional roles of molecularly defined cell types.
source: Finally, we also envision this approach to facilitate combined measurements of neuronal activity, for example, by calcium and voltage indicator imaging or electrophysiology measurements, with transcriptomic profiling of individual cells to reveal the functional roles of molecularly defined cell types.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an envisioned application.

source: Because our thick-tissue 3D MERFISH method uses commercially available spinning disk confocal microscopes and we have made our image analysis code publicly available, we anticipate that this method can be readily adopted by many laboratories.
